H1.text: A metro map shows a whole city with a few coloured lines. A stick figure shows a person with five strokes. And a chemist can draw a big molecule with one zigzag.

H2.text: Three drawings. Each one drops the details you already know.

H3.text: Aarav sees it at his study table. He is copying octane from the board. Eight carbons, eighteen hydrogens, every single bond.

H4.text: He is still drawing when the teacher wipes the board. But her own notes show octane as one zigzag line.

H5.text: Same molecule, much faster. By the end, you will read and write all three kinds of drawings.

P1.text: So how do chemists draw a molecule?

P2.text: The first way is the complete structural formula. Every atom is written, and every bond is a dash.

P3.text: A single bond is one dash. A double bond is two dashes. A triple bond is three.

P4.text: The second way is the condensed formula. We drop the dashes and group the atoms on each carbon, like C H three.

P5.text: The third way is the bond line formula. Only lines. Carbon and hydrogen are not written at all.

P6.text: Three drawings of one molecule. Like a full photo, a short note, and a quick sketch.

S1.text: Let's draw butane all three ways, on our molecule bench.

S2.text: First, four carbon atoms join in a row with single bonds.

S3.text: Each carbon needs four bonds. So hydrogens fill every free hand. Ten hydrogens in all. This is the complete formula.

S4.text: Now squeeze. Each end carbon holds three hydrogens, so we write C H three. Each middle carbon holds two, C H two.

S5.text: That gives C H three, C H two, C H two, C H three. The condensed formula.

S6.text: Now drop every letter. Keep only the carbon to carbon bonds, as a zigzag. Three lines. This is the bond line formula of butane.

B1.text: Here are the rules of bond line drawings.

B2.text: Every corner is a carbon, and every line end is a carbon.

B3.text: Hydrogens are not drawn. Each carbon has four bonds, so the missing bonds are all to hydrogen.

B4.text: Other atoms, like oxygen or chlorine, are always written. A double bond is drawn as two lines.

B5.text: Rings are just shapes. A triangle is cyclopropane. A pentagon is cyclopentane. A hexagon is cyclohexane.

D1.text: Now let's read a bond line drawing, link by link.

D2.text: Link one. Count corners and line ends. That gives the carbons.

D3.text: Link two. At each carbon, count the lines drawn.

D4.text: Link three. Hydrogens on that carbon equal four minus the lines. A double line counts as two.

D5.text: Link four. Add the hydrogens on every carbon.

D6.text: Link five. Write the formula. This branched drawing has five carbons and twelve hydrogens. C five H twelve.

C1.text: But paper is flat, and molecules are not. Methane is a tetrahedron. How do we show depth?

C2.text: Chemists use wedges. A plain line lies in the page.

C3.text: A solid wedge comes out of the page, towards you. A dashed wedge goes behind the page, away from you.

C4.text: Side by side, the flat drawing hides the shape. The wedge drawing shows it. Two bonds in the page, one towards you, one away.

C5.text: Pause and think. In this wedge drawing, which hydrogen points away from you?

C6.text: The one on the dashed wedge! Dashes go behind the page. Solid wedges come towards you.

T1.text: Remember this. Three drawings, one molecule. The atoms never change.

W1.text: Now, one worked example. Here is a bond line drawing with O H at one end. Find its condensed and molecular formula.

W2.text: Step one. Count corners and ends. Five carbons. The O H is written, so it is joined to the last carbon.

W3.text: Step two. The far end carbon has one line, so three hydrogens. The three middle carbons have two lines each, so two hydrogens each.

W4.text: Step three. The carbon next to O H has two lines, so two hydrogens. Three, plus six, plus two. Eleven hydrogens on carbon.

W5.text: Step four. Add the hydrogen in O H. Twelve hydrogens in all.

W6.text: Condensed, it is C H three, C H two four times, O H. Shorter still, C H three, bracket C H two, four, O H. Its formula is C five H twelve O.

X2.text: Students count only the corners of a zigzag. Three lines, two corners, so they say two or three carbons.

X3.text: Wrong. The two line ends are carbons too. Three lines means four carbons. That is butane.

E1.text: Where is this asked? Boards and entrance tests ask you to turn a bond line drawing into a formula, expand a condensed formula, or read a wedge drawing.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A hexagon with one double line inside is drawn in bond line form. What is its molecular formula? Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is B. C six H ten.

A2.text: Six corners, so six carbons. Four of them have two lines each, so two hydrogens each. That is eight.

A3.text: The two carbons of the double bond have three lines each, so one hydrogen each. Eight plus two is ten.

A4.text: A, C six H twelve, forgets the double bond. C, C six H six, is benzene with three double bonds. D is a chain, not a ring.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Write the condensed formula of propane.

Y3.text: Two. In a bond line drawing, what does a corner stand for?

Y4.text: Three. What does a dashed wedge tell you?
